alerts.rationale: recv_object deserializes bytes received over the distributed CPU process group directly with pickle.loads, which can execute attacker-controlled pickle payloads. The source is selected as a rank in the group, but no authenticity or safe-deserialization check is applied, so a compromised or otherwise untrusted peer rank can exploit this primitive; send_object confirms these bytes are peer-transmitted.

`recv_obj` directly passes bytes retrieved from the shared TCPStore to `pickle.loads` without validation (lines 114–120); anyone able to write to that store under the expected key can supply a pickle that executes code when deserialized. The API is explicitly for inter-process metadata and normal sends serialize Python objects, but that does not establish that the store contents are protected from an untrusted participant.

The received bytes come directly from a TCPStore entry and are passed to pickle.loads without validation; the same class writes broadcast payloads into that store, and its documented purpose is communication among ranks. Any party able to write/poison the store entry (for example, a compromised or unauthorized participant with access to the store) can trigger pickle deserialization behavior in the receiving process, so this is a potential vulnerability rather than a safe constant-data use.

The image-processor loader passes the supplied component model identifier/path directly to Hugging Face `from_pretrained` without a `revision` argument, so a remote Hub repository resolves its mutable default revision. The caller-level loader also routes that path into this customized loader, with no pinning or validation shown in these lines.

The processor loader passes component_model_path directly to Hugging Face from_pretrained with no revision argument, so a Hub repository resolves to its current default revision rather than a pinned commit; the adjacent native-loading path explicitly uses server_args.revision (lines 149–159), but this customized processor path does not. Thus a mutable or attacker-controlled Hub model reference can change what is downloaded between loads.

The tokenizer loader passes component_model_path to Hugging Face AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained without forwarding server_args.revision, unlike the native loaders that explicitly pass that revision (lines 154–159, 163–167). Thus when the component path identifies a Hub repository, loading follows the mutable default revision rather than a pinned/configured revision; this is a real unpinned download path.

The fallback explicitly invokes unrestricted pickle-based loading (`weights_only=False`) when a file triggers the legacy-tar RuntimeError, so a crafted checkpoint can execute code during deserialization. The files come from a local model directory and are globbed as `.bin`/potentially `.pt` inputs without integrity or trust validation; the comment's claim of trusted HuggingFace sources is not enforced (the code even asserts the path is local).

The scheduler directly unpickles the final frame of any multipart message received on its ROUTER socket, before validating the decoded object. That endpoint is a TCP endpoint derived from the configured host, so a party able to reach it can submit a crafted pickle and execute code in the scheduler process; the internal-client expectation does not make the pickle safe.

The calls use `model_dir` plus fixed `tokenizer`/`clip_text_encoder` subpaths (lines 22–27), consistent with loading components from a local model bundle rather than selecting a Hub repository revision. A repository-wide search found no call sites for `HunyuanClip`, so there is no demonstrated attacker-controlled Hub download path for this flagged call.

The argument is constructed as a model subdirectory (`model_dir/clip_text_encoder`), rather than passed as a bare Hugging Face repository ID; a missing local path does not identify a valid Hub repo in this form. Thus this call does not present an unpinned remote model download risk as written (lines 25–27).

The pickle is read from a newly created temporary directory after a locally launched subprocess has completed successfully; the parent itself supplies the subprocess input via cloudpickle, and the result is used for internal model inspection. No attacker-controlled file or network data is shown reaching this deserialization, so the flagged load is trusted local IPC in this flow (lines 161–186, 200–203).

The HTTP image URL is passed directly to requests.get with streaming enabled and no timeout, and image_path can come from the caller's request field; a slow or nonresponsive remote host can therefore hold up image loading/request processing indefinitely. The scheme check only selects URL handling and imposes no host or timing constraint.

`load_video` accepts HTTP(S) URLs and performs `requests.get(..., stream=True)` without a timeout, then iterates the response body; the request can therefore hang indefinitely on an unresponsive or stalled remote endpoint. The image-path validation invokes this loader for `.mp4` inputs without imposing a timeout or other bound on the request.

The pipeline passes its configured model_path directly into Transformers `from_pretrained` with no revision pin (lines 121–123); the path originates from the pipeline's model path configuration (qwen_image.py lines 116–125). If configured as a Hugging Face repository, this resolves the default moving revision, so downloaded model code/weights are not pinned against repository changes.

The broker binds a TCP socket on all interfaces and directly passes each received client-controlled payload to pickle.loads with no authentication or validation, allowing a reachable client to trigger pickle deserialization effects. The broker is started as part of the HTTP server lifespan (lines 49–50), so this is an active network-facing path.

The flagged deserialization consumes an arbitrary reply received from the configured scheduler endpoint and immediately executes pickle loading without authentication or validation; a malicious or compromised service reachable at that endpoint can provide a pickle payload that executes code in the client process. The scheduler endpoint host is configurable, so this is not intrinsically restricted to a trusted in-process value.

The receiver deserializes the byte payload received from the distributed process group directly with pickle.loads, with no validation or trust check (lines 46–57). Because the payload is supplied by the source rank, a compromised or otherwise attacker-controlled rank can send a pickle that executes code during loading; the callers use this for inter-rank request/batch synchronization (scheduler.py lines 294–315; parallel_executor.py lines 38–53, 80–86).

The wrapper forwards arbitrary kwargs but neither it nor its remote callers supply a revision; model IDs are passed through as selected by the caller, and downloads consequently resolve the Hub's mutable default branch (lines 486-494, 694-711). This permits repository updates to change the downloaded model without a pinned revision, so the B615 finding is applicable for these model downloads.

The wrapper forwards arbitrary caller kwargs but does not require a revision, and the operational callers shown pass only model identifiers and download options; the Hub therefore resolves a mutable default branch/revision. Downloading code/model artifacts from that moving reference can silently change what is executed or loaded, so this is a genuine supply-chain pinning risk.

`read_records` directly unpickles every file with no validation, and the CLI accepts an arbitrary `--input-file` or scans an arbitrary `--input-folder` before calling it. Python pickle loading can execute attacker-controlled reconstruction code, so replaying a supplied or shared untrusted dump permits code execution; the documented request/crash dumps being produced internally does not make externally obtained files safe.

This is a local replay utility posting to a user-configured host, and the absence of a timeout can cause a replay worker to wait indefinitely but does not by itself expose untrusted input or create an exploitable security condition. The request is performed by the replay script in its worker and exceptions are caught, with no security-sensitive operation relying on timely completion (lines 83–87, 107–116).
